summary: Elvin Aghammadzada (DataRobot) presents skills as versioned, task-specific packages encoding workflow knowledge for AI agents. He identifies three layers in agent applications: UI (user-facing), system prompt and tool descriptions (model-facing), and data schema (data-facing), with bugs hiding in the latter two. The first challenge is context rot: despite frontier models promising 1M-5M token contexts, performance degrades after 25% usage. Documentation traffic from coding agents surged from 10% to 50% in one year, yet docs are written for human intuition, not model consumption. The speaker reframes platform moats, contrasting friction moats (defensive switching costs) with fluency moats (offensive, experience-driven loyalty). Skills create fluency moats by commoditizing the experience layer. Teachability emerges as a new platform evaluation criterion. The smart zone (first 40% of context) is where LLMs perform well; preloading instructions and MCP connections can fill this before any conversation begins. Skills solve this via progressive disclosure—loading only metadata initially and full capabilities at runtime. Fifteen MCP servers can consume over 100,000 tokens in tool definitions; skills reduce this approximately 10x. Skills metadata acts like database indexes, loaded on demand. This creates a mental model shift: instead of building separate agents per use case, one general-purpose agent can be customized with skills across industries. Skills and MCP are complementary, both from Anthropic. MCP defines actions without changing agent capabilities; skills customize how the agent thinks and reasons, enabling self-modification. Skills can expose or create MCP servers, making them complete packages. Use skills when the hard part is reasoning; use MCP for authentication, access control, and resource isolation requiring remote execution. Current agents typically use only a handful of tools, suggesting skills can replace MCP when a strong base reasoning model exists. Skills have three levels: front matter (<100 tokens, always loaded), markdown body (<5K tokens, loaded on activation), and scripts (executable or reference code). The ecosystem includes 26+ platforms and 100,000s of skills with emerging marketplaces. Open Agent's repository became the most-starred project, demonstrating self-healing and self-evolving skills. However, research shows LLM-generated skills hurt performance by consuming more tokens and reasoning time. Key risks include prompt injection from unverified skills, lack of process isolation compared to MCP, and marketplace verification gaps akin to early NPM. Closing thoughts emphasize context as a budget, skills complementing MCPs, and that skills are software requiring versioning, evaluation, and testing.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Speaker outlines the talk structure: skills, context challenges, and the emerging ecosystem around skills including open cloud initiatives.

sections.title: Three Layers of Agent Applications
sections.summary: Describes three layers in agent tech apps: UI (user-facing), system prompt and tool descriptions (model-facing), and data schema (data-facing). Bugs typically hide in the second and third layers.

sections.title: The Context Window Problem
sections.summary: Challenges the promise of infinite context windows. References a context rot paper showing performance degrades after 25% usage. Long conversations with multiple tool calls cause frontier models to perform poorly, repeating earlier mistakes.

sections.title: Documentation Challenge
sections.summary: Documentation traffic from coding agents increased from 10% to 50% in one year, but docs are written for human intuition, not model consumption, requiring a context engine to bridge the gap.

sections.title: Moats and Teachability
sections.summary: Contrasts friction moats (defensive SaaS-era switching costs) with fluency moats (offensive experience-driven loyalty). Skills commoditize the experience layer. Introduces teachability as a new platform evaluation criterion.

sections.title: Standards and Context Engineering
sections.summary: Compares current LLM/agent ecosystem to pre-React web development. Defines context engineering as minimizing information flow to the LLM at the right time. Identifies M times N problem of connecting agents to all context sources simultaneously.

sections.title: Skills and Progressive Disclosure
sections.summary: Introduces smart zone (first 40% of context) and dumb zone (beyond 40%). Warns that preloading instructions and MCPs can fill 40% before conversation begins. Skills solve this via progressive disclosure. 15 MCP servers consume over 100,000 tokens in tool definitions; skills reduce this approximately 10x.

sections.title: Skills Metadata as Indexes and Mental Model Shift
sections.summary: Skills metadata acts like database indexes, loaded on demand at runtime. This creates a mental model shift: instead of building separate agents per use case, one general-purpose agent can be customized with skills across industries and domains. Skills are becoming a framework across platforms like Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot.

sections.title: Skills vs MCP Comparison
sections.summary: Both skills and MCP are from Anthropic and solve different problems. MCP defines actions without changing agent capabilities; skills customize how the agent thinks and enables self-modification. Skills can expose or create MCP servers. Use skills when the hard part is reasoning; use MCP for authentication, access control, and resource isolation requiring remote execution. Current agents use only a handful of tools, suggesting skills can replace MCP with a good base reasoning model.

sections.title: Three-Level Skill Structure
sections.summary: Skills have three levels: front matter (<100 tokens, always loaded to agent system prompt), markdown body (<5K tokens, loaded on activation by LLM), and scripts (executable code in Claude Code or reference examples on other platforms). Only the front matter burns context at runtime; the body loads on demand.

sections.title: Skills Ecosystem and Open Agent
sections.summary: 26+ platforms support skills (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI). 100,000s of skills exist with marketplaces. DataRobot published an open source agent skills repository. Open Agent became the most-starred repository, surpassing Winix and React, demonstrating self-healing and self-evolving skills with sub-agents for context management.

sections.title: Risks of LLM-Generated Skills
sections.summary: Research shows LLM-generated skills hurt performance by consuming more tokens and reasoning time. Risks of self-writing, self-executing skills include prompt injection, lack of process isolation (unlike MCP), and unverified marketplaces similar to early NPM.

sections.title: Closing Thoughts
sections.summary: Context is a budget—longer context doesn't mean better performance. Skills complement MCPs. A skill is only as good as the human who wrote it. Skills are software requiring weeks to build, versioning, evaluation, and testing.
